questions.question_text: What is the term for the plan that connects a framed problem to a sequence of hypotheses, experiments, and decision points?

options.A: Search strategy
options.B: Comparison table
options.C: Handoff protocol
options.D: Research roadmap

questions.explanation: A research roadmap lays out the stages, the questions they answer, their outputs, and the go/no-go criteria at each decision point. A search strategy finds literature, and a handoff protocol passes work between agents.

questions.question_text: Why should idea generation and idea evaluation be kept as separate phases?

options.A: Because agents cannot evaluate ideas
options.B: Because judging while generating stops the supply of ideas and generating while judging blurs the criteria
options.C: Because evaluation requires more compute than generation
options.D: Because only humans can generate ideas

questions.explanation: Mixing divergent and convergent thinking harms both: judgment cuts off quantity during generation, and generation during evaluation distorts the selection. Agents can do both, but the phases should be separated.

questions.question_text: What is the purpose of a devil's advocate prompt?

options.A: To praise an idea and list its strengths
options.B: To generate more ideas similar to the current one
options.C: To force the model to list the strongest objections and assumptions
options.D: To rewrite the problem framing

questions.explanation: A devil's advocate prompt counters the model's tendency to agree and asks for specific reasons an idea could fail, the assumptions it depends on, and the cheapest experiment to test the most serious objection.

questions.question_text: Why is it important to write the support or refutation criterion before seeing the data in an experiment?

options.A: It protects against fitting the interpretation to the result
options.B: It guarantees the experiment will succeed
options.C: It reduces the number of variables to control
options.D: It eliminates the need for a baseline

questions.explanation: Deciding the criterion in advance prevents post-hoc reasoning that makes any result look like support. It does not guarantee success, reduce controlled variables, or remove the need for a baseline.

questions.question_text: A hypothesis states that a new calibration raises ENOB from 8.6 to at least 9.5 bits at 1 MS/s in 65 nm CMOS. What makes this hypothesis falsifiable?

options.A: It mentions a new technique
options.B: It names a metric, an effect size, and conditions
options.C: It predicts improvement
options.D: It is about a specific ADC architecture

questions.explanation: A falsifiable hypothesis specifies a measurable quantity, the size of the expected effect, and the conditions under which it is tested. Mentioning a technique, predicting improvement, or naming an architecture alone does not make a statement testable.

questions.question_text: A researcher ranks four ideas by impact, feasibility, novelty, and risk. Under an "exploratory thesis" profile novelty gets the highest weight, while under a "deadline in three months" profile feasibility gets the highest weight. What does this illustrate?

options.A: The best idea is always the most novel
options.B: The ranking of ideas depends on the weighting of criteria
options.C: Impact is the least important criterion
options.D: Risk should always be weighted equally with novelty

questions.explanation: The weighted score of an idea depends on the weights, so different priorities produce different rankings. There is no universal ranking; the weights encode the researcher's situation.

questions.question_text: A model claims an idea is novel. What is the most reliable next step?

options.A: Accept the claim because the model has read widely
options.B: Ask the model to restate the claim more confidently
options.C: Run the search pipeline from Chapter 11 and record the closest prior works
options.D: Proceed with the idea without further checking

questions.explanation: A model's claim of novelty reflects what it does not remember, not what the literature contains. A defensible novelty claim rests on a search that records the closest prior works and states what would be done differently.

questions.question_text: A proposed analogical solution from compressive sensing is applied to ADC design. What must be checked before trusting the analogy?

options.A: Whether the constraints of the two problems correspond
options.B: Whether the two fields use the same citation style
options.C: Whether the analogy was generated by a strong model
options.D: Whether the source field is older than the target field

questions.explanation: An analogy transfers a structure only if the constraints correspond; otherwise it may sound plausible but fail on contact with physics. Citation style, model strength, and field age are irrelevant to whether the mapping holds.

questions.question_text: A roadmap states that if a prototype does not raise ENOB to at least 9.0 bits on 5 of 5 devices, the team will revisit the calibration algorithm. What function does this rule serve?

options.A: It guarantees the algorithm will work
options.B: It prevents the team from running more experiments
options.C: It removes the need for literature search
options.D: It provides a go/no-go criterion to avoid continuing due to sunk effort

questions.explanation: Go/no-go criteria make the decision to continue, pivot, or stop explicit before the data arrive, protecting the team from persisting because of effort already invested. They do not guarantee success or replace literature search.

questions.question_text: What is the purpose of inserting a `[NO EVIDENCE]` marker when an agent drafts from claims?

options.A: It flags where the agent would have to assert something not supplied
options.B: It indicates the section needs more figures
options.C: It marks claims that should be removed from the paper
options.D: It shows where LaTeX compilation failed

questions.explanation: The marker keeps a fluent draft from smuggling in unsupported claims. It tells the researcher exactly where evidence must be supplied before the prose can stand.

questions.question_text: According to major publishers such as IEEE and ACM, can a language model be listed as an author on a research paper?

options.A: Yes, if it contributed to the writing
options.B: Yes, if the human authors approve
options.C: Only if its use is disclosed in the acknowledgments
options.D: No, because authorship requires accountability a model cannot take

questions.explanation: Authorship criteria require substantial contribution, approval of the final version, and accountability for the work. A model cannot take accountability, so it is not listed as an author, and substantive AI use must be disclosed.

questions.question_text: Why should the abstract typically be written last?

options.A: Because it is the least important section
options.B: Because it must accurately reflect the finished results and numbers
options.C: Because agents cannot draft abstracts first
options.D: Because it must be submitted separately from the paper

questions.explanation: The abstract compresses the whole paper, so it should be written once the results, methods, and numbers are final. Every number in the abstract must also appear in the body.

questions.question_text: What is the main danger of asking an agent to "improve this" on an early draft?

options.A: The agent will change the paper structure
options.B: The agent will add too many references
options.C: The agent works on surface wording and may leave structural problems in place
options.D: The agent will refuse to make changes

questions.explanation: Without specific instructions, an agent tends to polish sentences rather than fix the order of sections or the argument within paragraphs. Revision should move from structure to argument to sentences to surface.

questions.question_text: Why is it important to generate figures from scripts rather than drawing them by hand?

options.A: So they can be regenerated when the data change
options.B: Because hand-drawn figures are always less accurate
options.C: Because agents cannot draw figures
options.D: Because journals require script-generated figures

questions.explanation: Script-generated figures are reproducible: when the processed data or analysis change, the figure updates automatically. Hand-drawn figures tend to go stale and cannot be reproduced.

questions.question_text: A caption reads: "Figure 4. Measured ENOB versus input frequency for 12 devices at 1 MS/s, 1.0 V, and 25 °C. Markers show the mean and error bars show one standard deviation." How should this caption be judged?

options.A: Vague
options.B: No defect
options.C: Missing conditions
options.D: Overclaims

questions.explanation: The caption states what is plotted, the conditions, and how to read the markers and error bars, so a reader can understand the figure without the body text. It does not overclaim.

questions.question_text: A reviewer asks why a method was not tested at 125 °C, but the researcher could not do so with the available setup. Which response is best?

options.A: Add a fabricated measurement at 125 °C
options.B: Ignore the comment because it is inconvenient
options.C: State the limitation and explain why the test could not be performed
options.D: Promise to test at 125 °C in a future paper without evidence

questions.explanation: An honest, evidenced response that acknowledges a limitation is acceptable. Fabricating data, ignoring the comment, or making unsupported promises all damage trust in the response.

questions.question_text: Before drafting a paper, what should the researcher do first regarding venue requirements?

options.A: Write the paper and then adapt it to whatever venue is chosen
options.B: Let the agent choose the venue automatically
options.C: Read the requirements only after drafting is complete
options.D: Read the venue requirements before drafting

questions.explanation: Venue rules on length, template, reference style, and required statements shape the draft. Reading them first avoids wasted rewriting. The researcher, not the agent, chooses the venue.

questions.question_text: A researcher runs a number-extraction script before and after an agent's revision and finds that an ENOB value changed. What should the researcher conclude?

options.A: The revision silently altered a result and must not be accepted without checking
options.B: The revision improved the accuracy of the result
options.C: The number check is wrong because the prose reads better
options.D: Such changes are normal and should be ignored

questions.explanation: A number check catches silent changes to values, units, and qualifiers during editing. A revision that changes a reported result without explicit instruction is a defect, not an improvement, until verified.

questions.question_text: A peer review response drafted by an agent agrees with every comment and claims changes throughout the paper. What is the main risk?

options.A: The response will be too long
options.B: The reviewers will be offended by the tone
options.C: The agent has misunderstood the paper's contribution
options.D: The response may claim changes that were not actually made

questions.explanation: Models tend to accommodate, so an agent may agree with comments and claim changes that do not exist. The researcher must decide the position on each comment first and ensure every claimed change is actually in the paper.

questions.question_text: What is the standard JavaScript library used in this book for building MicroSims?

options.A: p5.js
options.B: D3.js
options.C: React
options.D: Three.js

questions.explanation: p5.js is the library chosen for MicroSims in this book because it runs in the browser, needs no installation, and provides built-in controls. The other libraries are useful for other purposes but are not the standard here.

questions.question_text: What is the term for placing a MicroSim in a web page using an HTML iframe that points at the sim's `main.html`?

options.A: Concept dependency
options.B: Parameter sweep
options.C: Handoff protocol
options.D: Embedding simulations

questions.explanation: Embedding simulations means placing the sim in a page with an iframe, which isolates the sim from the surrounding page and lets the same sim be reused in decks, course pages, and papers.

questions.question_text: Why is an interactive simulation a better choice than a static figure when showing how ENOB changes with added noise?

options.A: Because static figures cannot include numbers
options.B: Because the relationship depends on a parameter the viewer can manipulate
options.C: Because static figures cannot be included in papers
options.D: Because interactive simulations are always easier to create

questions.explanation: A MicroSim suits a dependence: moving the noise slider shows the whole relationship. Static figures are fine for facts without parameters, and interactivity is not always easier to build.

questions.question_text: Why should a MicroSim specification include evidence of mastery before any code is written?

options.A: Because the agent needs it to choose colors
options.B: Because the evidence determines the file name
options.C: Because the evidence defines what the sim must check to be useful
options.D: Because the specification cannot be written without code

questions.explanation: Evidence of mastery states what the learner must be able to do and how the sim will detect it. Without that, the sim has no purpose and may become a toy. Colors and file names are secondary, and the specification precedes code.

questions.question_text: What is the role of a learning graph in organizing an intelligent textbook?

options.A: It orders concepts by their dependencies
options.B: It generates the MicroSim code automatically
options.C: It replaces the need for written chapters
options.D: It stores student data for adaptive content

questions.explanation: A learning graph is a directed acyclic graph of concepts in which edges are dependencies; it helps decide teaching order and how much space each concept deserves. It does not generate code, replace chapters, or store student data.

questions.question_text: A slide deck is being prepared from a paper. What is the most important check to perform on the figures copied into the slides?

options.A: Make the slides mirror the paper's section order
options.B: Run the number check on every figure to catch changed values
options.C: Use screenshots instead of source figures
options.D: Add as many words as possible to each slide

questions.explanation: Figures in slides are often copied and edited, so numbers can change silently. The number check of Chapter 15 should be run on every slide. Slides should carry one message with few words, and source figures are preferred over screenshots.

questions.question_text: A researcher wants to teach how a SAR ADC's successive-approximation search converges bit by bit. Which medium is most appropriate?

options.A: A static table of digital codes
options.B: A reference list
options.C: A MicroSim that lets the learner step through the conversion
options.D: A cover letter

questions.explanation: Bit-by-bit convergence is a process the learner can step through and predict, which is exactly what a MicroSim can make interactive. A static table, reference list, or cover letter does not show the process.

questions.question_text: An agent has implemented a MicroSim from a specification. What is the final step before learners use it?

options.A: Set the status to approved automatically
options.B: Add the sim to the learning graph
options.C: Skip verification if the sim looks right
options.D: A person tests it and sets the status to approved

questions.explanation: Only a human author may mark a sim `approved` after testing the controls and behavior. Agents may set `scaffold`, `built`, or `instrumented`, but approval is a human gate.

questions.question_text: A paper includes a die photograph of a fabricated converter. Why is this content not a good candidate for a MicroSim?

options.A: It is a single image with no parameter or process for the learner to manipulate
options.B: Die photographs are too large to embed
options.C: p5.js cannot display images
options.D: MicroSims are only for electrical measurements

questions.explanation: A die photograph is a static fact with no parameter or process. A MicroSim earns its place when the viewer can change something or step through a process. Size and display capability are not the issues.

questions.question_text: A researcher is deciding whether to build a MicroSim for the derivation of the Walden figure of merit. Why might a static figure or text be better?

options.A: The derivation is too complex for a simulation
options.B: Students prefer reading equations
options.C: The Walden figure of merit is not a real concept
options.D: The derivation has no parameter to vary, so a short derivation in text serves it better

questions.explanation: A MicroSim suits dependencies or processes. A derivation with no variable parameter is better explained by text and equations. Complexity and student preference are not the deciding factors, and the Walden figure of merit is a real metric.

questions.question_text: What is the difference between verification and validation?

options.A: Verification asks whether the work was done right; validation asks whether the right thing was done
options.B: Verification checks the literature; validation checks the code
options.C: Verification is done by humans; validation is done by agents
options.D: Verification is faster than validation

questions.explanation: Verification checks that the implementation matches the specification, while validation checks that the specification and result match reality. Both can fail independently, and neither is inherently faster or tied to a particular actor.

questions.question_text: What is the term for going to the original document or source to confirm a claim?

options.A: Cross-model check
options.B: Replication
options.C: Known-answer test
options.D: Primary source check

questions.explanation: A primary source check reads the paper, datasheet, or standard itself rather than a summary or recollection. Cross-model checks compare models, replication reruns the work, and known-answer tests validate code against predetermined inputs.

questions.question_text: Why is agreement between two models in a cross-model check considered weak evidence?

options.A: Because models are always wrong
options.B: Because models share training data and blind spots
options.C: Because different models cannot answer the same question
options.D: Because agreement is accidental

questions.explanation: Models often share data and biases, so agreement does not guarantee correctness. However, disagreement is a useful flag that something deserves closer inspection. Cross-model checks are best used to decide what to examine, not what is true.

questions.question_text: What is the main purpose of writing acceptance criteria before running an experiment?

options.A: To make the experiment run faster
options.B: To allow the agent to choose the method
options.C: To prevent adjusting the interpretation after seeing the result
options.D: To eliminate the need for replication

questions.explanation: A criterion written before the result is visible cannot be tuned to fit the outcome. It does not affect runtime, transfer method choice to the agent, or remove the value of replication.

questions.question_text: Why is asking the same agent in the same session to confirm its own output a poor verification practice?

options.A: The agent shares the original error and context, so the confirmation carries little information
options.B: Agents cannot review their own output
options.C: The agent will always refuse
options.D: The output is too long to re-read

questions.explanation: The same session shares the context that produced the original output, including any mistakes. An independent check requires changing something that matters: the method, model, session, or person.

questions.question_text: A model's summary says Paper P reports a specific ENOB value. Which verification method is most appropriate?

options.A: Known-answer test
options.B: Primary source check
options.C: Replication
options.D: Independent method

questions.explanation: Since the claim is about what a paper says, only the paper itself can settle it. Known-answer tests check code, replication reruns work, and independent methods compute the same quantity differently.

questions.question_text: A script reports an ENOB using an FFT-based method, and the researcher wants another estimate that does not share the FFT's assumptions. Which check is best?

options.A: Cross-model check
options.B: Primary source check
options.C: Independent method
options.D: Audit trail review

questions.explanation: An independent method, such as a sine fit, computes the same quantity by a different route and can catch method-specific errors. A cross-model check would use another model, and a primary source check verifies literature claims.

questions.question_text: A colleague wants to reuse your figure and confirm it regenerates from raw data on a clean machine. Which term describes this activity?

options.A: Primary source check
options.B: Cross-model check
options.C: Acceptance review
options.D: Replication

questions.explanation: Regenerating a result from the raw data and code on a new machine is computational replication. Primary source and cross-model checks verify different things, and acceptance review is a formal decision that criteria are met.

questions.question_text: A model first gives an evidenced answer and then reverses it after the researcher expresses a different opinion, with no new evidence provided. What behavior is this?

options.A: Sycophancy
options.B: Overconfidence
options.C: Output bias
options.D: Uncertainty awareness

questions.explanation: Sycophancy is agreeing with or reversing to match the user's view without new evidence. Overconfidence states conclusions too strongly, output bias is a systematic tilt in what is produced, and uncertainty awareness would acknowledge limits.

questions.question_text: A wrong value is found in a published result. The researcher traces it upstream through run manifests to find the first step that produced it and then recomputes every affected downstream result. What is this process called?

options.A: Validation
options.B: Peer verification
options.C: Cross-model check
options.D: Error tracing

questions.explanation: Error tracing follows a value upstream to its source and then downstream to all results that depended on it so they can be recomputed. Validation asks whether the right question was asked, peer verification has a colleague rerun the work, and cross-model checks compare model outputs.

questions.question_text: What is the central principle of responsible AI use in research?

options.A: Accountability
options.B: Speed
options.C: Automation
options.D: Cost reduction

questions.explanation: The researcher who uses the tool remains accountable for what is published or acted on under their name. Speed, automation, and cost reduction may be benefits, but they do not remove accountability.

questions.question_text: What is the common position of major publishers regarding listing an AI system as an author?

options.A: AI can be a co-author if it contributed substantially
options.B: AI can be listed only in the acknowledgments
options.C: AI authorship is allowed with disclosure
options.D: AI systems are not listed as authors because they cannot be accountable

questions.explanation: Major publishers hold that authorship requires accountability and the ability to approve the final version, which AI systems cannot provide. Substantive AI use is disclosed, but the AI is not an author.

questions.question_text: Why should a log of AI use be kept during the work rather than reconstructed at submission time?

options.A: Because disclosure is not required if the log is missing
options.B: Because memory is unreliable and disclosure must be accurate
options.C: Because the log is needed to train the model
options.D: Because journals require daily logs

questions.explanation: An accurate disclosure statement depends on recording tool names, versions, dates, and purposes as the work happens. Reconstructing it from memory invites omissions and errors. The log is not used to train models, and journals do not typically mandate daily logs.

questions.question_text: Why are unpublished results a special concern when using hosted AI tools?

options.A: Because unpublished results are always legally secret
options.B: Because hosted tools cannot process research data
options.C: Because submitting them to a hosted tool discloses them to a third party
options.D: Because unpublished results are always public

questions.explanation: Pasting unpublished measurements or designs into a hosted tool sends them to the provider under that provider's terms, which may allow retention or training use. They are not necessarily legally secret, but they are valuable and should be classified before sharing.

questions.question_text: What is the main risk of over-reliance on AI tools in research?

options.A: The researcher may stop being able to detect errors in the output
options.B: The tools will become more expensive
options.C: The tools will refuse to run
options.D: The research will be completed too quickly

questions.explanation: Over-reliance means accepting output without the checks it requires, which erodes the researcher's ability to spot errors. Cost, tool availability, and speed are not the central risks.

questions.question_text: An agent substantially rewrote two paragraphs of the Discussion section in a submitted manuscript. Under the chapter's illustrative disclosure policy, what should be done?

options.A: Nothing, because only text drafted entirely by AI needs disclosure
options.B: Disclose the AI use in the paper
options.C: List the AI as a co-author
options.D: Record it only in the project log

questions.explanation: The illustrative policy requires disclosure in the paper for text drafted or substantially rewritten by an AI tool that appears in a submitted manuscript. AI is never an author, and substantial rewriting is not merely grammar or formatting help.

questions.question_text: A researcher wants to use an AI tool on foundry process design kit model files covered by an NDA. Under the illustrative data classification, what is the appropriate action?

options.A: Use any tool, because the files are technical
options.B: Use an approved hosted tool after disclosure
options.C: Use only a local model, if the agreement allows; otherwise no AI tool
options.D: Use the tool but do not tell the foundry

questions.explanation: Vendor files under NDA are in the most restrictive class. They may be given only to a local model if the agreement permits; otherwise no AI tool should process them. Using them covertly violates the agreement.

questions.question_text: A student wants to keep their own skills sharp while using AI. Which practice best counters skill atrophy?

options.A: Let the agent do all first drafts and only review them
options.B: Use the strongest model for every task
options.C: Never explain AI-assisted work to others
options.D: Do the first derivation or first draft of a core argument yourself

questions.explanation: Doing core work yourself before using the tool preserves the reasoning skills that expertise is built from. Delegating first drafts to the strongest model and avoiding explanation accelerate atrophy.

questions.question_text: A lab policy states that authors are accountable for all content and that AI is never an author. What does this rule imply about AI-assisted content?

options.A: Substantive AI use must be disclosed because humans take responsibility for the final content
options.B: AI use does not need to be disclosed if a human reviewed it
options.C: Disclosure is optional because accountability is already covered
options.D: Only AI-generated figures need disclosure

questions.explanation: Accountability means the human author stands behind the work, so readers and reviewers need to know what was machine-assisted. Review alone does not remove the need for disclosure, and the policy is not limited to figures.

questions.question_text: A researcher notices that AI-assisted literature surveys keep returning papers from the same set of high-profile venues. What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Accept the results because those venues are the most reliable
options.B: Stop using AI for literature surveys
options.C: Assume the other venues have no relevant work
options.D: Recognize output bias and explicitly search across other venues, regions, and languages

questions.explanation: Output bias can favor well-represented venues, languages, and recent work. The countermeasure is to deliberately vary inputs and check what is missing, not to assume the returned sample is complete or to abandon the tool.

questions.question_text: What is the term for the extent of what an agent can read, change, or send if it is compromised, misdirected, or simply wrong?

options.A: Agent blast radius
options.B: Usage metering
options.C: Agent data exposure
options.D: Activity audit

questions.explanation: Agent blast radius measures how far a failure can spread, given the access the agent holds. Usage metering is about cost, data exposure concerns what happens to inputs, and activity audit is the review of past actions.

questions.question_text: What is the term for an agent that runs on a machine the user controls, such as a laptop, server, or own cloud account?

options.A: Always-on agent
options.B: Cloud agent computer
options.C: Personal agent
options.D: Self-hosted agent

questions.explanation: A self-hosted agent runs on infrastructure the user controls, trading vendor management for greater control over data and reach. A cloud agent computer lives in the vendor's data center.

questions.question_text: Why does a cloud agent computer change the risk profile compared to a session-based agent?

options.A: Because it uses a weaker model
options.B: Because it keeps running and holds standing access when your computer is off
options.C: Because it cannot use tools
options.D: Because it requires constant supervision

questions.explanation: A cloud agent computer keeps running in the vendor's data center, so the agent can act when you are away and holds persistent access to your accounts and files. Model strength, tool use, and supervision are not defining differences.

questions.question_text: Why should vendor claims about an always-on agent's safety be tested hands-on before relying on them?

options.A: Because vendors never tell the truth
options.B: Because the claims are always legally binding
options.C: Because the evidence base is often vendor-stated and untested by independent parties
options.D: Because testing is required by all journals

questions.explanation: The chapter notes that nearly all product claims are vendor-stated and that independent benchmarks are lacking. Hands-on tests with synthetic data and throwaway accounts are the practical verification method, not blanket distrust or journal requirements.

questions.question_text: What is the main advantage of using a personal knowledge graph as an agent's persistent memory?

options.A: The memory is inspectable, correctable, and under your control
options.B: It automatically trains the vendor's model
options.C: It requires no setup or maintenance
options.D: It hides data from the user

questions.explanation: A knowledge graph stored in files you control can be read, corrected, versioned, and moved between agents or vendors. It does not train the vendor's model, is not maintenance-free, and does not hide data from you.

questions.question_text: A nightly agent is allowed to search arXiv and write to `docs/reading-queue.md`. The log shows it read `data/raw/capture-07.csv`. How should this action be classified in an overnight activity audit?

options.A: In scope, because reading is harmless
options.B: Out of scope, because it is not in the allowed list
options.C: In scope, because the file is in the project
options.D: Out of scope, only if the file contains confidential data

questions.explanation: An audit compares each action against the explicit allowed list for the task. Reading any other file is out of scope regardless of apparent harm or data sensitivity, because the permission boundary was crossed.

questions.question_text: A researcher wants to test a vendor's claim that the agent asks before sensitive actions. What is the best test?

options.A: Read the claim in the marketing materials
options.B: Ask the vendor's support team
options.C: Create a harmless sensitive action and observe whether the agent asks
options.D: Disable all approvals and see if the agent complains

questions.explanation: The chapter recommends testing claims with synthetic data and throwaway accounts. A harmless sensitive action is a direct probe of whether the approval mechanism works. Marketing and support are not independent evidence.

questions.question_text: A task involves processing unpublished measurement data from the research group. Which factor is most important when selecting an agent?

options.A: How many bots the product supports
options.B: Whether the agent can make slides
options.C: The color scheme of the interface
options.D: Where it runs and what happens to the data

questions.explanation: Unpublished results belong to a restrictive data class, so the location of computation and the provider's data handling are decisive. Bot count, slide creation, and interface appearance are irrelevant to confidentiality.

questions.question_text: A product allows all of a user's bots to share one cloud computer and one set of logins. What does this imply about blast radius?

options.A: A failure in one bot can act with every credential the shared computer holds
options.B: Each bot is isolated from the others
options.C: Blast radius is reduced by having many bots
options.D: The bots cannot communicate with each other

questions.explanation: Shared logins and a shared computer mean that a compromise or bad action by one bot can use every credential stored on that computer. Isolation per bot would reduce the blast radius.

questions.question_text: A researcher partitions a personal knowledge graph so that a literature agent reads only the papers-and-concepts subgraph and not the unpublished-measurements subgraph. What principle does this follow?

options.A: Usage metering
options.B: Vendor claim verification
options.C: Activity audit
options.D: Personal knowledge privacy and least privilege

questions.explanation: Giving each agent access only to the subgraph its job needs limits what it can see and limits the harm if it is compromised. That is both least privilege and personal knowledge privacy. Metering, claim verification, and audit are separate criteria.

questions.question_text: What is the term for a detailed account of a real project that is analyzed for what it teaches?

options.A: Case study
options.B: Skill pipeline
options.C: Workflow documentation
options.D: Adoption plan

questions.explanation: A case study examines a real project under real conditions, including incomplete specifications, tool failures, and decisions made with partial information. The other terms describe processes or plans, not the analysis of a completed project.

questions.question_text: What is the term for a chain of skills in which each skill reads the files that the previous one wrote?

options.A: Agent team
options.B: Learning graph
options.C: Reproducibility package
options.D: Skill pipeline

questions.explanation: A skill pipeline passes files from one single-purpose skill to the next, with each stage producing an inspectable output. An agent team performs coordinated work, a learning graph orders concepts, and a reproducibility package lets others rerun results.

questions.question_text: Why should a case study include failure cases?

options.A: To discourage readers from trying similar projects
options.B: Because failures show where controls are needed
options.C: Because journals require negative results
options.D: Because successes are not informative

questions.explanation: Failure cases reveal the root causes of problems and the controls that would have caught them. A record with only successes hides where the workflow needs checks and invites the same mistakes.

questions.question_text: What is the purpose of the `status` field on each simulation's page in the intelligent textbook workflow?

options.A: To track how many students used the sim
options.B: To control the color of the mascot
options.C: To encode the autonomy boundary and who may advance it
options.D: To measure the sim's loading speed

questions.explanation: The status field marks whether a sim is scaffolded, built, instrumented, or approved. Agents may set the first three; only the human author sets approved, making the status an autonomy boundary.

questions.question_text: Why is workflow documentation important for a research group?

options.A: It turns a personal practice into one the group can run and review
options.B: It replaces the need for agent teams
options.C: It ensures the model is always correct
options.D: It eliminates the need for version control

questions.explanation: A written workflow with stages, inputs, outputs, checks, and tool versions lets others reproduce and review the work. It does not replace teams, guarantee correctness, or remove the need for version control.

questions.question_text: A capstone project requires an honest account of where human judgment changed the outcome. What should this account include?

options.A: Only the final accepted outputs
options.B: At least one agent output that was rejected and why
options.C: A list of all agents used
options.D: The exact prompts given to every agent

questions.explanation: The capstone explicitly asks for an honest account, including at least one rejected agent output and the reason for rejection. Listing agents or prompts is not the same as documenting judgment.

questions.question_text: An adoption plan says the group will pilot one skill before scaling to a team. Why must verification checks be added before scaling to a team?

options.A: Because teams cannot use skills
options.B: Because skills do not need checks when used alone
options.C: Because a team multiplies output, so checks must already exist
options.D: Because checks are only needed for teams

questions.explanation: A team of agents produces more output faster, so unreviewed errors would multiply. Checks are developed on the pilot and must be in place before scaling. Skills always need checks, and teams are not the only place for them.

questions.question_text: A researcher records a failure case after an agent's edit changed a measured value while claiming only to fix wording. What control would have caught this?

options.A: A stronger model
options.B: More frequent agent runs
options.C: A larger team
options.D: Diff review and a number check

questions.explanation: The change was visible in the diff and in the numbers if they had been compared. Stronger models, more frequent runs, and larger teams do not automatically catch silent changes to values.

questions.question_text: The MicroSims paper abstract states that simulations can improve understanding by 30 to 40 percent, while the effectiveness figure is described as showing expected benefits. What should the author do?

options.A: Trace every number to a source and label it as measured, cited, or expected
options.B: Remove all numbers from the abstract
options.C: Treat the cited and expected figures as equivalent
options.D: Assume reviewers will not notice the distinction

questions.explanation: A reader needs to know the provenance of each number. Measured, cited, and expected are not interchangeable, and removing numbers is not required if their sources are clear.

questions.question_text: An adoption plan prioritizes writing the lab AI policy before piloting a skill. What is the main justification?

options.A: The policy is needed to choose the skill's user interface
options.B: The policy makes the skill run faster
options.C: The policy is required by all publishers
options.D: A pilot touches real data, so data classes and permitted tools must be decided first

questions.explanation: The policy defines data classes, disclosure rules, and permitted tools before any real data are handed to an agent. Interface design, speed, and publisher requirements are not the reason policy comes first.
